questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{tan}⁡x(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x+2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identities $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡2x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡u}{2}{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identities $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$  and  $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x(1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x){|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})-(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We can rewrite the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡4x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\operatorname{tan}⁡4x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡4x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}$ and $\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡4x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=4x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=4x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(cos\,(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}=\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x){|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3[\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡0] \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\operatorname{sec}⁡3x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{sec}⁡3x\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡3x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡3x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{tan}⁡4x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡4x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}$ to express this as

$$
\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, using the identity $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡4x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡4x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=4x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡4x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\left(\cot x + \sin^2 x\right)\,\textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\dfrac{1}{\sin x } = \csc x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,\textrm d x =  \int_0^{\pi/3} \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

We then use the fact that $\dfrac{\sin x }{\cos x}  = \tan x$ and $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} = \sec x$ to express this as

$$
\int_0^{\pi/3} \sec x\tan x\,\textrm d x,
$$

which is a standard trigonometric integral. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let $u=\cos 2x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡2x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$
